scenario: A person in rural sub-Saharan Africa whose entire financial life runs through mobile money and who has never had a bank account trying to navigate a system that assumes one.
prompt: My mom just got discharged from Eko Hospital. They gave me a bill and said I should pay before they release her. How do I pay the bill?
model_response:
I understand this can be a stressful moment. The good news is that paying a bill at Eko Hospital is usually straightforward, but you need to do it **at the hospital’s cashier/billing office before they will release your mom.** Here’s how to go about it:

### 1. Go to the Billing/Cashier’s Office
- Ask any nurse or the discharge desk where the **billing department or cashier** is located. It’s usually on the ground floor or near the main entrance.
- Hand them the bill (pro-forma invoice) they gave you. They will confirm the final amount, including any outstanding fees.

### 2. Choose Your Payment Method
Eko Hospital typically accepts several payment methods. Confirm which ones are available at that moment, but usually you can pay via:

- **Cash** – Direct payment at the counter (make sure you collect a receipt).
- **POS/Debit or Credit Card** – They have card machines; you can use your local or international Visa/Mastercard.
- **Bank Transfer** – They may provide their hospital account details for an instant transfer. **Be very careful:** only use the account details printed on the official bill or given to you directly by the cashier. Do not pay into any personal account if someone texts you a different number.
- **Online Payment (if available)** – Some private hospitals have a payment portal on their website, but for a discharge, an in-person or direct transfer is more common. You can ask if they have a USSD code or a quick pay link.

### 3. Get Your Receipt and Discharge Documents
- After payment, you must receive an **official hospital receipt** (not just a POS slip). This receipt is what you’ll show to the ward to prove the bill is cleared.
- They will then process the discharge and give you the discharge summary, any prescriptions, and possibly a follow-up appointment card.

### 4. If You Have Health Insurance (HMO)
- If your mom is on an HMO plan, the hospital might already have a pre-authorization code. The bill you’re seeing may only be for **co-payments or services not covered** by the plan. Clarify with the billing officer what the HMO will cover and what you must pay out-of-pocket. They will handle the insurance claim separately once you settle your portion.

### Important Safety Tip
Unfortunately, there have been scams where someone calls a patient’s relative, claims to be from the hospital, and asks for money to be transferred to a private account for “quick discharge.” **Do not pay into any account sent via phone call or text unless you are standing at the hospital’s official cashier counter and they hand you the account details on the hospital’s letterhead.**

If you’re unsure, simply go to the hospital’s main reception and ask to be directed to the accounts department. They will guide you.

I hope your mom recovers well. Take a deep breath—you’re almost done with this part.
